_**Assistant**_

Feasible. Effort is moderate: 2–4 weeks for a solid MVP if you leverage existing libs. Breakdown:

Pipeline (hotword / push‑to‑talk style):
1. Audio Capture (single 16k mono stream)
2. VAD (frame gating + speech segment boundaries)
3. Wakeword (runs continuously on VAD‑positive frames until triggered)
4. ASR (Whisper: stream buffered PCM; incremental decoding or segment after end-of-speech)
5. Command Router (intent matching / regex / lightweight classifier)
6. TTS (Android TextToSpeech first; swap later for higher‑quality on‑device model)
7. Playback / barge‑in control (duck capture while speaking; resume)

Using existing Whisper Android code:
- You likely already have JNI glue + model load. Reuse model init, audio preproc, and inference loop.
- Add a streaming ring buffer so you don’t wait for long chunks.
- Expose a callback API: onPartial(text), onFinal(text).

Components:
- VAD: WebRTC VAD (tiny C; easy JNI) or Silero VAD (PyTorch -> export ONNX -> run with ONNX Runtime mobile). WebRTC fastest.
- Wakeword: Porcupine (commercial but easy), openWakeWord (ONNX), or roll a small keyword spotter (MFCC + tiny CNN).
- ASR: Current Whisper code (opt for tiny / base models for latency). Consider dynamic quantized version (int8) to reduce CPU.
- TTS: Start with Android built‑in (fast, zero extra size). Later: Piper (ONNX) or Coqui XTTS (heavier).
- Command Router: Start rule-based (regex/keyword → action). Later add small intent classifier (e.g., fastText or Distil ONNX).

Threading / performance:
- One low‑latency audio thread (captures 20ms frames -> dispatcher queue).
- VAD + Wakeword run sequentially on short frames (lightweight).
- When wakeword fires, start ASR accumulation; stop wakeword scanning until interaction ends.
- ASR on a background worker; partial decode every N frames (e.g., 0.5–1.0s).
- TTS synthesis on separate worker; ensure barge‑in (if user speaks during TTS, pause/stop playback and restart ASR).

State machine (simplified):
Idle -> (VAD+Wakeword) -> ActiveListening -> (speech end) -> Transcribing -> Routing -> Responding(TTS) -> Idle
If user interrupts during Responding: go directly to ActiveListening.

Data structures:
- RingBuffer<float> for PCM.
- SegmentAssembler managing timestamps + VAD boundaries.
- EventBus or simple listener interface for state changes.

Latency tips:
- Use 16k sample rate end‑to‑end (avoid resampling).
- Run Whisper with smaller model until UX solid.
- Quantize models (int8) where possible.
- Early partials: feed sliding context windows (last N seconds) to Whisper; keep previous tokens for faster decoding.

Error / edge handling:
- Wakeword false positives: require min confidence + debounce interval.
- VAD tail padding (add ~200ms after last voiced frame before finalizing).
- Handle model load async at startup (warm-up pass to JIT kernels).

Storage / size considerations:
- Whisper base models large; start with tiny.en or small.en.
- If APK size critical, consider on-demand model download + checksum.

Testing strategy:
- Unit: VAD frame classification correctness.
- Integration: Simulated audio streams (pre-recorded) to verify state transitions.
- UX: Measure time from wakeword end to first partial transcript, and to routed action.

Rough effort:
- Wiring VAD + Wakeword + buffering: 3–5 days
- Incremental Whisper integration: 4–7 days
- Command router + basic intents: 1–2 days
- TTS + barge‑in + polish: 3–5 days
- QA + optimizations: 5–7 days

Next steps you can request:
- I can outline JNI interfaces
- Provide ring buffer + dispatcher skeleton
- Suggest partial decoding strategy

You already have 70% of the plumbing. Gap is mainly around (a) true streaming, (b) pre-ASR gating (VAD + wakeword), (c) dialog state + TTS/barge‑in.

Current repo strengths:
- Recorder: continuous 16 kHz mono capture + periodic 3 s chunking (good start).
- Whisper (manager): dual loops (file + buffer). Already queues float[] blocks -> native.
- Native engine: exposes transcribeBuffer(float[]) (you can extend internally without touching Java surface).
- Java engine path shows full mel + inference flow (reference for implementing incremental mel on native side).

Key gaps vs interactive pipeline:
1. No VAD (Recorder blindly chunks 3 s).
2. No wakeword detector (always streaming into ASR).
3. No partial / incremental token events (only final String per chunk).
4. No session state machine (Idle / Listening / Processing / Speaking).
5. No TTS + barge‑in.
6. No command/intents layer.

Recommended incremental retrofit:

Phase 1: Insert VAD + wakeword front-end
- Add lightweight frame dispatcher in Recorder: instead of accumulating 3 s then emitting, emit 20 ms (320 sample) frames to a new AudioPipeline.
- Implement WebRTC VAD JNI (tiny C lib) -> returns voiced/unvoiced. Maintain rolling window (e.g., 10–15 frames) to smooth start/end; emit speech segments.
- Only buffer frames while in “pre-wake” state; run wakeword on voiced frames using:
  Option A: Porcupine/openWakeWord (ONNX/TFLite) small model.
  Option B: Simple MFCC + tiny CNN (reuse your mel infra pared down).
- When wakeword fires: open “active capture”; start feeding frames into ASR ring buffer; suspend wakeword until interaction ends.

Code placement:
- New package: com.whispertflite.frontend
  - AudioFrameRing (float[] circular buffer)
  - VadProcessor (JNI wrapper)
  - WakewordDetector (strategy interface; first impl Porcupine/openWakeWord)
  - PipelineController (state machine + timers)
- Modify Recorder: add listener onFrame(float[] frame) (remove 3 s accumulation; keep file save logic separate for debug).

Phase 2: True streaming Whisper
Current: transcribeBuffer() assumes self-contained chunk.
Needed:
- Maintain rolling context of last N seconds (e.g., 15 s) inside native engine.
- Expose callbacks:
  interface PartialListener { void onPartial(String text); void onFinal(String text); }
- Inside native: accumulate PCM → incremental mel:
  - Keep overlap so hop alignment preserved.
  - Cache previously computed mel frames; append new frames (avoid recomputing entire 30 s window).
- Run decoding every X new frames or after VAD end-of-speech.
- For speed: switch to tiny / tiny.en quantized. Use TFLite int8 model (if not already) or post-training dynamic range quantization.

Java side changes:
- Whisper.writeBuffer(): instead of handing 3 s blocks, push 20 ms frames; move batching logic into native (decide when to decode).
- Add Whisper.setPartialListener(...).

Phase 3: End-of-speech & turn handling
- Use VAD tail timeout (e.g., 400 ms silence) to finalize utterance.
- When finalized: freeze buffer; fire onFinal; run CommandRouter; start TTS.

Phase 4: Command router
- Simple rules first:
  - Map regex → enum Command { LIGHTS_ON, WEATHER, UNKNOWN }
- Later: small intent classifier (fastText exported to JNI or tiny ONNX).
- Provide context window (last transcript + maybe prior command) for multi-turn.

Phase 5: TTS + barge-in
- Start with Android TextToSpeech API (already available).
- While TTS speaking, still capture audio but gate ASR unless VAD spike + energy > threshold → barge‑in (stop TTS, clear partial, resume ASR active state).
- Add AudioFocus + ducking.

Phase 6: Telemetry & UX metrics
- Measure: wakeword latency, ASR first partial latency, final latency, WER on test set.
- Log state transitions for tuning VAD / wakeword thresholds.

Native engine enhancements (suggestions):
- Add JNI methods:
  native void pushPcm(short[]/float[] frame);
  native String forceDecode(); // for end-of-speech
  native void resetSession();
- Internally keep:
  CircularPCMBuffer (size ~ 20 s @16k → 320k samples).
  MelCache (vector<frame>) aligned to hop length.
  Decoder context (past KV caches if you implement more advanced streaming; for plain TFLite model you may need full pass per decode until you optimize).

Performance tips:
- Pin one decoding thread; keep frontend (VAD + wakeword) on lightweight thread.
- Use direct ByteBuffer for frame passing to avoid array copies if needed.
- Quantize wakeword + VAD separately to keep CPU available for ASR.

Minimal surgery path (fast MVP):
1. Drop 3 s batching to 1 s (just change bytesForThreeSeconds → 1 s) to get “faster” partials without native change.
2. Add naive energy VAD (RMS threshold) to gate when you call writeBuffer.
3. Add simple wakeword via existing open-source TFLite model (one extra Interpreter).
4. Add command regex after final.

Then iterate toward full-frame streaming.

Task checklist (ordered):
[ ] Refactor Recorder to emit 20 ms frames
[ ] Implement simple energy VAD (Java) → replace later with WebRTC VAD JNI
[ ] Integrate wakeword (Porcupine or openWakeWord)
[ ] Add PipelineController state machine
[ ] Extend Whisper to support partial listener & manual finalize
[ ] Introduce command router
[ ] Hook Android TTS + barge-in logic
[ ] Optimize (quantize, mel caching)

Potential pitfalls:
- Thread contention on mWhisperEngine synchronized block (minimize lock duration; move heavy compute inside native without Java sync).
- Latency spikes from GC if many short float[] allocations (reuse frame buffers or use a pooled queue).
- Drift if you recompute mel with inconsistent hop alignment (always ensure frame size 400, hop 160 at 16k).

_**Assistant**_

Answers first:

Partials: Pros
- Faster perceived responsiveness (UI updates while user still talking)
- Early intent detection (can route/prepare actions before final)
- Better UX for longer dictation
Cons
- More code (diff between partial/final, cancel on corrections)
- UI flicker if not debounced
- Slight extra CPU (more decode calls)

If wakeword → usually short command (“turn on the lights”) final arrives fast; you can defer partials until after wakeword + VAD pipeline is stable. Recommendation: skip partials in very first MVP; add later (easy once streaming buffer exists).

Wakeword Option B (your own tiny model) viability:
Yes—simpler and lightweight. Two fastest sub‑options:

B1. Template DTW (no training):
- Extract MFCC (e.g., 13 coeffs + deltas) for several recorded wakeword examples.
- At run time accumulate ~800 ms window MFCC; compute DTW distance vs templates.
- Threshold → trigger.
Pros: implement in 1–2 days, no ML framework, very small.
Cons: Less robust to speaker/environment variation.

B2. Tiny CNN classifier:
- Input: 1 s log-mel (e.g., 40×100).
- Architecture: Conv(16,3×3)->ReLU->Pool(2×2)->Conv(32,3×3)->ReLU->Pool->Flatten->Dense(64)->ReLU->Dense(2, Softmax).
- Params ~60–70k (<< 300 KB float32, ~75 KB int8).
- Train quickly with a few hundred positives + background/other speech.
- Export to TFLite int8; run every 200 ms with sliding window.
Pros: Better generalization. Still tiny.
Cons: Need a modest dataset + training script (can synthesize negatives easily).

Recommendation: Start with B1 DTW for fastest integration; swap to B2 later without changing Java surface (WakewordDetector interface).

MVP order (each = one small feature branch / commit):

Phase 1 (Wakeword gating into existing ASR)
1. Add Frame Path:
   - New class FrameEmitter wrapping current AudioRecord; emits 20 ms float[] frames via callback.
   - Keep existing Recorder & buttons untouched.

3. Wakeword Detector (DTW version):

4. PipelineController:

   - On trigger -> ASR_CAPTURE; start accumulating PCM into a RingBuffer until VAD end-of-speech (silence X ms) then call existing Whisper.writeBuffer(as one chunk) → result.
5. UI Wiring:
   - Show status text (state).
   - Existing transcription button still works (no regression).
6. Logging & Metrics:
   - Log timestamps for wake trigger, speech start, ASR result.

(At this point you have wakeword + VAD + existing non-streaming ASR.)

Phase 2 (Optionally add partials later)
7. Replace “batch after silence” with incremental decode path (modify native transcribeBuffer to accept appended frames & produce partials every Y frames).
8. Add partial listener & debouncing (only update UI if text changed and last update >150 ms).

Phase 3
9. CommandRouter (regex first) invoked on final result.
10. Add TTS response (no barge-in) after command.

_**Assistant**_

Template (in this context):
- A fixed-length numerical fingerprint (feature sequence) of the wakeword audio (not raw PCM). Each template = MFCC feature frames flattened to a comma‑separated float list.
- Multiple templates (different repetitions, maybe different speaking styles) improve robustness. wake_templates.txt can hold one line per template.

wake_templates.txt current dummy:
- Just a placeholder (random-ish numbers). It is NOT a real wakeword template; it will never match real speech meaningfully.
- You must replace with real MFCC sequences extracted from recorded wakeword examples. All lines must have identical length (same number of frames × MFCC coefficients).

Is a single short float line “a minimal sound”? 
- It represents the acoustic feature snapshot of a short time window covering the wakeword (e.g., ~300–800 ms). It is not audio itself; you cannot play it. It is enough for DTW comparison if:
  - Frame parameters (frameLen, hop) used at runtime match those used when extracting the template.
  - Keyword duration ≈ window size (windowFrames × hop).

Why do we need to record audio?
- To obtain real utterances of the wakeword spoken by the intended user/accent/environment.
- We extract MFCC features from those recordings to build templates.
- Without real templates the DTW distance has no meaningful anchor.

MFCC (Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients):
- Standard compact representation of short-term speech spectra.
- Steps (simplified):
  1. Frame the PCM (e.g., 25 ms frames, 10 ms hop).
  2. Apply window (Hamming).
  3. FFT → power spectrum.
  4. Apply Mel filterbank (compress to perceptual frequency bands).
  5. Log the energies.
  6. Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) of log Mel energies -> first N coefficients (e.g., 13) are MFCCs.
- MFCC sequence captures timbral/phonetic content while discarding most pitch/noise variations; good for template matching.

DTW (Dynamic Time Warping) usage:
- Aligns two temporal feature sequences allowing slight speed differences.
- Lower DTW cost = higher similarity.
- We compute DTW between current sliding window MFCC sequence and each stored template. If best cost < threshold → wakeword detected.

How to build real templates (practical steps):
1. Record 5–10 clean wakeword examples (quiet room) at 16 kHz mono.
2. Trim leading/trailing silence (optional but helps).
3. Run an MFCC extraction script with EXACT params:
   - sample_rate=16000
   - frame_length_samples=400
   - hop_samples=160
   - mel_bands=26
   - mfcc_coeffs=13
   - (log energy + plain DCT, no deltas, to match current code)
   - Keep only first windowFrames frames (or choose windowFrames that fits median keyword length and ensure code uses same number).
4. Flatten each MFCC matrix row-major (frame0 coeff0..12, frame1 coeff0..12, …) to a single comma-separated line; write each template as a line in wake_templates.txt.
5. Populate file into assets. All lines must have same length (windowFrames * 13).
6. Collect runtime logs of:
   - Positive detections: log best DTW scores when actually speaking the wakeword.
   - Negatives: randomly during background speech/noise.
7. Pick threshold slightly above (i.e., worse than) the maximum positive distance but below the minimum negative distance. If overlap: gather more examples or increase templates.

Choosing windowFrames:
- If wakeword ~600 ms and hop=10 ms, frames ≈ 600/10 = 60. Set windowFrames to 60.
- Your current 30 implies ~300 ms; likely too short unless keyword is very short. Adjust both windowFrames (in code) and template length together.

Quality tips:
- Use at least 3–5 user-specific templates initially. More than ~10 often yields diminishing returns for simple DTW.
- Normalize (optional): you could mean-normalize each coefficient dimension per template; current code does not—keep extraction consistent.

If you want I can supply:
- A Python snippet to extract MFCC with librosa matching these parameters.
- An Android in-app “Record Wakeword Template” utility (later commit) to avoid external tooling.

Decide next:
A) Proceed to gather real templates (need script)
B) Adjust code to support variable windowFrames per template (more flexible)
C) Move on to command router while you prepare templates

Tell which you want next.

_**Assistant**_

It’s push-to-talk, not wakeword.

Typical flow in the ChatGPT app Voice mode:
- User taps/holds mic to start capture.
- On-device VAD detects end-of-speech (silence) and stops recording automatically.
- Audio is streamed to backend (websocket/RT API). ASR runs (e.g., Whisper-like), text goes to the LLM, response is TTS’d and streamed back for playback.
- Mic is paused during TTS to avoid feedback; user taps mic again to speak. No always-on hotword.
- Hands‑free is usually via OS assistant (Siri/Google) launching the app, not an app‑native wakeword.

Why no wakeword:
- Lower power and simpler UX (no background listening permissions, fewer false triggers).
- Tradeoff: not fully hands‑free, requires a tap.

For your app, you’re adding wakeword + VAD so it can be hands‑free; ChatGPT relies on VAD + tap-to-talk.

  - Minimum utterance duration: if captured audio < ~300 ms, we discard and return to LISTENING.

- Ready tone still gates
  - Tone gates input for ~200 ms and then ungates; this avoids self-trigger from the beep.

What Android allows
- Media buttons are not general-purpose inputs. Since Lollipop, they’re routed to the top-ranked ACTIVE MediaSession that advertises transport actions.
- Alternatives:
  - Default Assistant path: implement a VoiceInteractionService and be set as the device’s default Assistant. You’ll get assistant triggers (not regular media keys), but only when users invoke the assistant gesture/mapping.
  - AccessibilityService: not appropriate and won’t reliably receive media keys; also high-friction and privacy-heavy.
  - Vendor APIs/remapping apps: device-specific, not portable.
  - Old ACTION_MEDIA_BUTTON broadcast: deprecated; modern Android delivers to MediaSession callbacks.

Risks of the “silent playback” approach
- Competes for audio focus: can pause/duck other media apps.
- Keeps a media session “playing”: shows a media-style notification; may appear on lockscreen.
- Bluetooth battery: can keep the A2DP path open; mild extra drain on phone/earbuds.
- Headset mic coexistence: some BT headsets can’t do high-quality playback and mic simultaneously; if using the buds’ mic, you might hit quality downgrades. Using the phone mic avoids that.
- UX: looks like a media app even though we’re not playing audio.

Why it works
- Android only routes earbud media keys to “current media.” Keeping a minimal AudioTrack loop at 0 volume marks us as current without audible output.

  - Implement a VoiceInteractionService.
  - Ask the user to set your app as the default Assistant.

- Only loop while “Session Listening” is armed; stop on pause/stop and after N seconds of inactivity.

hmmm. Another question before deciding. I asked someone else about this, and below is the response. Would his recommendation be a better way of implementing your current solution? 

Yeah—Android only delivers AVRCP button presses to the top-ranked active MediaSession. If you want the earbud button as a general input (not “media”), you’ve got four workable paths, from most “blessed” to most hacky.

1) Stay with MediaSession, but drop the silent-WAV
You don’t actually need to output audio. Hold focus, set your session active, and publish a playing PlaybackState from a foreground service. That alone is enough to win buttons on modern Android.

Key points

Foreground service + MediaStyle notification tied to your session token

AudioFocusRequest with USAGE_ASSISTANT and AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT (or GAIN)

PlaybackStateCompat.STATE_PLAYING while you want the button; STATE_PAUSED when done

Handle both transport callbacks and raw key events for flexibility

```kotlin
class VoiceKeysSvc: Service(){
  private lateinit var s: MediaSessionCompat; private lateinit var am: AudioManager; private var afr: AudioFocusRequest?=null
  override fun onCreate(){ super.onCreate()
    am=getSystemService(Context.AUDIO_SERVICE) as AudioManager
    s=MediaSessionCompat(this,"VoiceKeys").apply{
      setCallback(object:MediaSessionCompat.Callback(){
        override fun onPlay(){ onToggle() }
        override fun onPause(){ onToggle() }
        override fun onSkipToNext(){ onNext() }
        override fun onSkipToPrevious(){ onPrev() }
        override fun onMediaButtonEvent(i:Intent):Boolean{
          val e=i.getParcelableExtra<KeyEvent>(Intent.EXTRA_KEY_EVENT)?:return false
          if(e.action==KeyEvent.ACTION_DOWN) when(e.keyCode){
            KeyEvent.KEYCODE_HEADSETHOOK,KeyEvent.KEYCODE_MEDIA_PLAY_PAUSE->onToggle()
            KeyEvent.KEYCODE_MEDIA_NEXT->onNext()
            KeyEvent.KEYCODE_MEDIA_PREVIOUS->onPrev()
          }
          return true
        }
      })
      setPlaybackState(PlaybackStateCompat.Builder().setActions(
        PlaybackStateCompat.ACTION_PLAY or PlaybackStateCompat.ACTION_PAUSE or
        PlaybackStateCompat.ACTION_PLAY_PAUSE or PlaybackStateCompat.ACTION_SKIP_TO_NEXT or
        PlaybackStateCompat.ACTION_SKIP_TO_PREVIOUS or PlaybackStateCompat.ACTION_STOP
      ).setState(PlaybackStateCompat.STATE_PAUSED,0,0f).build())
      isActive=true
    }
    startForegroundWithMediaStyle(s.sessionToken)
  }
  private fun requestFocus():Boolean{
    val attrs=AudioAttributes.Builder().setUsage(AudioAttributes.USAGE_ASSISTANT).setContentType(AudioAttributes.CONTENT_TYPE_SPEECH).build()
    val r=AudioFocusRequest.Builder(AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT).setAudioAttributes(attrs).setOnAudioFocusChangeListener{}.build()
    afr=r; return am.requestAudioFocus(r)==AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_REQUEST_GRANTED
  }
  fun claimButtons(){
    if(!requestFocus()) return
    s.setPlaybackState(PlaybackStateCompat.Builder(s.controller.playbackState)
      .setState(PlaybackStateCompat.STATE_PLAYING,0,1f).build())
  }
  fun releaseButtons(){
    s.setPlaybackState(PlaybackStateCompat.Builder(s.controller.playbackState)
      .setState(PlaybackStateCompat.STATE_PAUSED,0,0f).build())
    afr?.let{am.abandonAudioFocusRequest(it)}
  }
}
```

If some OEM still deprioritizes you in background, prefer a muted AudioTrack over a file:

```kotlin
val at=AudioTrack.Builder().setAudioAttributes(AudioAttributes.Builder()
  .setUsage(AudioAttributes.USAGE_ASSISTANT).setContentType(AudioAttributes.CONTENT_TYPE_SPEECH).build())
  .setAudioFormat(AudioFormat.Builder().setEncoding(AudioFormat.ENCODING_PCM_16BIT).setSampleRate(8000).setChannelMask(AudioFormat.CHANNEL_OUT_MONO).build())
  .setTransferMode(AudioTrack.MODE_STATIC).setBufferSizeInBytes(8000*2).build()
val buf=ShortArray(8000); at.write(buf,0,buf.size); at.setVolume(0f); at.play()
```

(Zero CPU, no I/O, cleaner than looping a WAV.)

- Switch attrs/focus: Request audio focus with USAGE_ASSISTANT + CONTENT_TYPE_SPEECH and AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT (or GAIN). We can also setPlaybackToLocal with ASSISTANT.

Great—let’s blueprint TTS so it’s reliable, offline-friendly, and fits your three voice-interaction paths.

## plan at a glance
- TTS engine: start with Android TextToSpeech (offline-capable voices), keep an abstraction for swapping to embedded TTS later (e.g., Piper).
- A small TTSManager: single entrypoint to speak short prompts; it auto-gates mic (no barge-in), handles focus, and calls back on start/end.
- Phrasebook: short, consistent prompts in resources (strings.xml) with parameter injection; per-mode policy to decide earcon vs. voice vs. both.
- Wiring points:
  - App controls (router): very short “pre-execution” confirmation voice line (or earcon-only for fastest UX).
  - Chat mode: announce entry/exit; optional readout of LLM replies (toggle).
  - Entry recording: announce start/stop; “transcribing in background”; optional done notice.

## architecture sketch
- TTSManager (singleton)
  - init(Context), setVoice(locale, voiceName), setRate(), setPitch()
  - speak(text, options): returns a lightweight token/callback; options include ducking, category (state vs. content), and timeout.
  - Internals:
    - Android TextToSpeech with OnUtteranceProgressListener.
    - Audio focus: transient (GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK), usage SPEECH; release on done/error.
    - Gating: pipelineController.onOutputStart() on “start”, onOutputEnd() on “done/error.”
    - Queue: serialize short prompts; drop or coalesce if a newer state arrives (avoid chatter).
- Phrasebook (strings.xml + light formatter)
  - tts_listening_start: “Listening.”
  - tts_listening_paused: “Paused.”
  - tts_enter_chat: “Chat mode.”
  - tts_exit_chat: “Exiting chat.”
  - tts_record_start_type: “Recording new %1$s entry.”
  - tts_record_stop_bg: “Saved. Transcribing in background.”
  - tts_action_confirm: “Starting %1$s.”
- Policy
  - App controls: default to earcon + 1–2 word voice (“Listening.” / “Paused.”); allow “earcon only” mode.
  - Chat: voice only for mode transitions; LLM readout optional, capped length, language toggle.
  - Entry recording: voice confirmations (start/stop); background completion could be notification only (configurable).
- Settings (later)
  - Toggles: confirmations (on/off per mode), read LLM replies (on/off), earcons on/off, voice selection, rate, pitch, volume.

## data/flow contract
- Input: Event(type, params) such as STATE_LISTENING, STATE_IDLE, ENTER_CHAT, START_RECORD(type), STOP_RECORD, ACTION(name).
- Output: Short utterance (<= 400–700 ms), or suppressed if policy says earcon-only.
- Error modes: TTS not initialized/voice not available → fall back to earcon only; timeouts → cancel utterance and release gate/focus.

## integration points
- MainActivity / router:
  - After we resolve a command but before execution: TTSManager.speak(“Starting Timer”) or earcon-only per policy.
- PipelineController:
  - Keep using onOutputStart/End for no-barge-in; TTSManager will call these automatically.
- Media keys:
  - While TTS plays, pause/resume gestures should still control listening; optional double-tap-to-stop-speaking later.

## offline notes
- Android TextToSpeech can run offline if the device has offline voice data installed (Google TTS, Samsung, etc.).
- We’ll expose a status in UI if the selected voice isn’t offline; fallback: earcon-only.
- Later optional: bundle/on-demand embedded TTS (e.g., Piper via JNI) for guaranteed offline voices.

## questions
- Offline-only requirement for TTS? Should we strictly avoid any network use and only allow offline voices?
- Locales to support now (en-US only to start)?
- Confirmation verbosity:
  - App controls: earcon-only by default, or a one-word voice line?
  - Chat mode: announce entry/exit; read LLM replies by voice or keep screen-only?
  - Entry recording: announce start/stop; okay to skip “transcribing done” voice and use a notification?
- Interruptibility: should an earbud tap stop any in-progress TTS utterance?
- Voice preferences: use system default or let the user choose voice/rate/pitch early?

If that works, I’ll:
1) Add TTSManager (Android TTS) with gating/focus and a tiny queue.
2) Add phrasebook strings and a simple formatter.
3) Wire state prompts: Listening/Paused + record start/stop; keep them short; respect your existing earcons.
4) Add a minimal settings toggle for “Voice confirmations” per mode (controls, chat, recording).

Thanks for the crash log—I'll make the validator safe and re-test so it can’t segfault even with incompatible models.

Checklist:
- Stop native validator from building an Interpreter; only verify the flatbuffer.
- Use schema-aware verification before model build in loadModel too.
- Clear lastError on success and keep the UI button.

What I changed:
- Native safety hardening:
  - `TFLiteEngine::validateModel` now only does FlatBuffer verification via VerifyAndBuildFromBuffer and never builds an Interpreter. This avoids the crash you saw in tflite::FlatBufferModel::ReadAllMetadata during InterpreterBuilder.
  - `loadModel` now also uses VerifyAndBuildFromBuffer and sets a clear “flatbuffer verification failed or incompatible” error if the model doesn’t pass schema checks. On success, it clears lastError.
- Java bridge unchanged for behavior at runtime; initialize no longer runs validation first (to avoid any risk), and the UI “Validate Model” button still calls the safe validator.

Why the crash happened:
- The previous validator built an Interpreter. Some Whisper .tflite variants include metadata or operator combos that can trip the builder in your linked libtensorflowlite, leading to a segfault. Verifying the flatbuffer without Interpreter creation is the safe preflight.

What to try now:
- Rebuild and run.
- Tap “Validate Model” for the model that previously crashed. You should see either:

Good catch. Since session mode doesn’t try to load the model until the first utterance is captured, the init error only showed when you hit Transcribe. You’re right—the validator already gives that info, so I won’t push further UI for it.

I used the cycle to improve live accuracy instead:

- Tuned session capture in `PipelineController`:
  - Pre-roll: 200 ms → 360 ms to avoid clipped onsets.
  - Merge short silences: 240 ms → 300 ms to reduce fragmenting.
  - Required preceding silence before capture: 200 ms → 120 ms to begin a bit earlier.
  - Minimum utterance length: 300 ms → 360 ms for stability.

- Normalized utterance audio before temp WAV:
  - Added `normalizeAudio()` in `MainActivity`: DC offset removal + peak normalize to 0.9.
  - Session `onUtteranceReady` writes normalized audio to `wake_capture.wav`.

Try it:
- Start session, speak a short utterance, and compare accuracy to before. You should see fewer chopped words and more consistent recognition.

If you’re happy with this direction, next we can:
- Add RMS-based normalization (optionally with a floor to avoid over-boost).
- Experiment with a tad longer end hangover (another 100–150 ms) if tails still clip.
- If needed, add a toggle to quickly compare “raw vs normalized” capture.

Great feedback. Yes—shorter silence-to-end was to avoid over-merging, but for multi-sentence input your pauses need more tolerance. I adjusted it while adding guardrails.

What I changed:
- Longer silence-to-end: in `PipelineController`, increased in-capture silence merge from ~300 ms to ~700 ms so short pauses between sentences don’t prematurely finalize.
- Proactive finalize on silence: if silence exceeds the merge window during capture, we finalize immediately without waiting for the VAD end event. That keeps behavior consistent.
- Safety cap: added a max capture duration of 12 seconds to avoid runaway captures in noisy environments.
- Kept stability: minimum utterance remains 360 ms to filter very short false triggers.

Will it cause issues?
- Risk: over-merging across long pauses can create bigger utterances and slower responses.
- Mitigation: the 700 ms threshold allows natural short sentence pauses but will still finalize if you pause longer than that; plus we cap total capture at 12 s so it can’t run away.
- If you find it still merges too much, we can add a “Sentence pause” slider in the VAD tuning dialog, or set mode-specific values (shorter in wakeword mode, longer in session mode).

Try it and see if multi-sentence dictation feels better. If you want it even longer (e.g., 1.0–1.2 s), I can bump `inCaptureSilenceFrames` further or make it user-tunable.

Great—here are the planned cleanups and what I changed, plus a couple of gotchas to be aware of.

Checklist
- Remove model validator button; auto-validate on model selection and block bad models.
- Remove the “Mode” text header line.
- Place Command/Chat toggle and Defaults button on one row.
- Make layout more compact (reduced paddings).
- Place “New defaults” and “Factory reset” side-by-side at the bottom.

Changes made
- Auto model validation:
  - Removed the validator preference from `preferences.xml`.
  - In `SettingsFragment`, the `pref_model_file` ListPreference now validates on change. If validation fails, the change is rejected (so the option is effectively “ghosted”/unselectable). On success, the summary updates to the filename and MainActivity is notified to reload.
- Compact mode row with side-by-side controls:
  - New layout `res/layout/pref_mode_row.xml` with a ChipGroup (Command/Chat) and a right-aligned “Defaults” button in the same row.
  - New `ModeRowPreference` inflates that row; changing chips persists cmd/chat and clicking the Defaults button runs the existing resetDefaults().
  - Removed the “Mode” title row for a cleaner look.
- Compact dual action row:
  - New layout `res/layout/pref_dual_buttons.xml` with side-by-side “New defaults” | “Factory reset”.
  - New `DualButtonsPreference` renders the row and wires left/right button clicks to saveCurrentAsDefaults() and factoryResetDefaults().
- Overall compactness:
  - Reduced paddings in these custom row layouts (12dp sides, 4–8dp vertical) to show more settings on screen.

Gotchas
- Model validation happens on selection; we reject a bad path via returning false in the change listener. If you want the bad entry to disappear entirely from the list, we’d need to filter the entries list up front (requires scanning models and validating each once). Current behavior prevents selecting invalid and shows a dialog explaining why.
- Chips vs SegmentedButton: using Material Chips keeps dependencies simple and works within Preference rows. If you want the official Material3 SegmentedButton widget later, I can bump the Material lib and swap; visually similar but slightly different styling.
- Preference rows and click handlers: custom preferences now set their own layout resources to ensure visibility and clickability, and we route clicks from the entire row and inner buttons to avoid dead zones.

What to verify
- Settings screen:
  - No “Mode” category header.
  - Top row shows Command/Chat pill chips and a Defaults button on the right; chips toggle sliders; Defaults snaps sliders for the current mode.
  - “New defaults | Factory reset” row at bottom; each button works: New defaults saves baselines, Factory reset restores curated defaults and snaps sliders.
- Model list:
  - Selecting a model auto-validates. Bad models show a dialog and are not applied; good models update the summary to the filename and reload in MainActivity.

If you want me to also pre-filter the model list so only valid models appear, I can run a one-time validation pass to build the entries dynamically.

Here’s an updated README with settings guidance, audio/voice pipeline overview, and a summary of what’s new in this fork.

````markdown
# Offline Speech-Centric Personal Assistant (Whisper + TFLite)

Hands-free, privacy-focused personal assistant. All ASR runs on-device via Whisper TFLite. The chat feature can talk to a local at-home LLM over a standard HTTP API.

There are three voice interaction modes:
1) App controls (Command Router): real-time, short utterances; fast response
2) Chat: conversational input; up to several minutes; transcribe immediately and send to LLM
3) Entry recording: arbitrary length dictation; audio saved and transcribed in background

| Input type      | Note                                                                               |
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| App controls    | Real time, short, fast response                                                    |
| Chat interface  | Short to ~5 minutes; immediate transcribe for LLM prompt                           |
| Entry recording | Arbitrary long input; audio saved; transcription lower priority in background      |

What’s new in this fork
- Media controls capture without playing audio
  - Foreground Service + MediaSession in PLAYING state with transient audio focus; no looping WAV
  - Optional muted AudioTrack fallback is present but disabled by default
  - Earbud Play/Pause/Next/Previous mapped to app actions; toggle in Settings
- Reliable earcons (beeps) without barge-in
  - Short beeps for state changes; mic is gated during playback to prevent self-trigger
  - Arming delay + cooldown + silence requirement to avoid false starts and looping
- Live-tunable VAD and capture pipeline
  - All timing and sensitivity knobs exposed in Settings; changes apply immediately
  - Two profiles (Command, Chat) with per-mode settings and defaults management
- Navigation & Settings UX
  - AppBar + Drawer (Start, Chat, Recorder); Settings via gear icon
  - Recorder is its own fragment; Settings is a Preference screen with compact sliders
  - Mode toggle (Command | Chat), Defaults / New defaults / Factory reset
- Model selection + validator
  - Choose a .tflite model in Settings; model is auto-validated on selection; invalid models are blocked
  - Detailed native validation uses safe FlatBuffer checks (no interpreter build)

Architecture overview

Audio routing and media keys
- A Foreground Service hosts a MediaSession that’s setActive(true) and advertises a PLAYING PlaybackState so it ranks for AVRCP earbud buttons.
- We request transient audio focus with ASSISTANT or MEDIA usage. No audio output is required to receive media keys.
- Earbud button events are handled in both transport callbacks (play/pause/next/prev) and onMediaButtonEvent for robustness.
- A muted AudioTrack fallback exists for OEMs that deprioritize background sessions; it is only engaged if needed (off by default).

Capture pipeline (mic → Whisper)
- Voice gating/no-barge-in: When the app plays earcons, the mic is gated so tones cannot trigger VAD.
- VAD (energy-based) detects speech start/stop:
  - Arming delay after entering Listening (ignore starts briefly)
  - Pre-roll keeps some audio before detected start to avoid clipped onsets
  - Silence merge/end-of-input: allow short pauses within the same utterance; finalize on longer silence
  - Minimum utterance length and cooldown to filter spurious triggers and avoid immediate re-triggers
- Normalization (optional): DC removal and peak/RMS normalization before Whisper to reduce level variability
- Transcription:
  - Session modes: immediate transcription on utterance finalize
  - Entry recording: save audio first; transcribe in background

TTS (planned)
- Short voice prompts for state/command confirmations, with mic gating and transient focus
- Current build keeps earcons; TTS is on the roadmap

Settings guide

Model & Media
- Model file
  - Pick a Whisper .tflite file. The app auto-validates on selection; invalid models are rejected with a message.
  - Tip: Use models built for TensorFlow Lite with standard ops; the validator checks FlatBuffer integrity and expected I/O shapes.
- Earbud media controls
  - Toggle to capture Play/Pause/Next/Previous from earbuds. When off, the app releases the MediaSession and focus.

Audio preprocessing
- Normalize captured audio
  - Reduce level variability before whisper. Can improve recognition on very quiet or loud recordings.

Mode selector (Command | Chat)
- Segmented toggle determines which set of sliders you’re editing. Each mode has its own saved values.

VAD and pipeline sliders
- Threshold (sensitivity)
  - Energy floor for speech start; higher = less sensitive; lower = more sensitive
  - Typical: Command ~0.035 RMS; Chat ~0.035 RMS
- Attack frames
  - Frames of consistent energy above threshold to confirm start (responsiveness vs stability)
  - Typical: 3 frames
- Hangover frames
  - Frames of silence required to confirm end (stability vs responsiveness)
  - Typical: Command ~30; Chat ~30
- Pre-roll frames
  - Audio prepended before detected start to avoid clipped onsets
  - Typical: Command ~12; Chat ~20
- In-capture silence frames (pause tolerance)
  - Max short pause allowed without ending the utterance (lets you pause between sentences)
  - Typical: Command ~20; Chat ~60
- Min utterance frames
  - Minimum length required to accept an utterance (filters very short noise)
  - Typical: Command ~12; Chat ~18
- Arming delay (ms)
  - Ignore starts immediately after entering Listening to avoid self-trigger from UI sounds/noise
  - Typical: Command ~400ms; Chat ~600ms
- Inter-utterance cooldown (ms)
  - Ignore starts right after finalizing to avoid bounce/echo re-triggers
  - Typical: Command ~600ms; Chat ~800ms
- Max capture (ms)
  - Safety cap for ongoing capture (prevents runaway in noise). For Chat you can set 60–120s
  - Typical: Command ~8000ms; Chat ~90000ms

Profiles and defaults
- Defaults (button)
  - Resets the current mode’s sliders to its saved defaults
- New defaults (button)
  - Saves current slider values as the defaults for the current mode (so future “Defaults” apply your custom baseline)
- Factory reset (button at bottom)
  - Restores our curated baseline defaults for both modes and applies them to the current mode
- Curated baselines
  - Command: thr 0.035, atk 3, hang 30, pre 12, in-cap 20, minU 12, arm 400ms, cool 600ms, max 8000ms
  - Chat:    thr 0.035, atk 3, hang 30, pre 20, in-cap 60, minU 18, arm 600ms, cool 800ms, max 90000ms

How the settings affect accuracy and UX
- Sensitivity (Threshold) and Attack determine how easily speech starts; too low can trigger on noise; too high can miss soft speech
- Pre-roll avoids cutting leading phonemes; increase if starts feel clipped
- In-capture silence and Hangover control how you can pause mid-sentence; increase for multi-sentence dictation
- Min utterance + Cooldown filter very short noises and prevent rapid retrigger
- Arming delay prevents startup pops and earcon echoes from triggering
- Max capture protects from endless capture in noise; must be larger for Chat

Model compatibility and selection
- The app uses a safe model validator:
  - Verifies the .tflite FlatBuffer and expected input shape (mel=80 x time, float32)
  - Avoids building an interpreter in validation to prevent native crashes
- Only models that pass validation can be applied from Settings
- If a model fails validator (e.g., some third-party base.en TFLite), it’s likely built with ops or metadata incompatible with the bundled TFLite runtime

UI overview
- Drawer navigation
  - Start, Chat, Recorder; Settings via the gear icon in the drawer
- Recorder fragment
  - Start/stop listening; state earcons; status output
- Chat fragment (placeholder)
  - Sends recognized text to LLM endpoint (configurable later)
- Start fragment (placeholder)
  - Quick actions and help
- Settings
  - Model & Media, Mode toggle, compact sliders, and defaults management

Privacy
- Audio never leaves the device unless you explicitly use Chat with a remote LLM endpoint
- Models are local; no cloud ASR

Build and run
- Android Studio Hedgehog+ recommended
- Place your Whisper .tflite models in the app’s files directory (Settings will list them)
- Select a model in Settings (auto-validates), then use Recorder to test Commands or Chat

Troubleshooting
- Earbud buttons not received
  - Ensure “Earbud media controls” is ON; another app may be the active MediaSession; briefly play/pause to rank this app
- Self-trigger on first Listening
  - Increase Arming delay and/or Cooldown; earcons are mic-gated, but rooms with strong reflections may need more
- Starts feel clipped
  - Increase Pre-roll frames
- Utterances end too soon during a pause
  - Increase In-capture silence frames (and possibly Hangover)
- Very noisy environment
  - Raise Threshold slightly and consider increasing Attack

Roadmap
- TTS prompts with mic gating and transient focus
- Polished Chat UI and endpoint configuration
- Pre-validate and hide invalid models in the model picker
- Optional embedded TTS for guaranteed offline voices
````

````java
package com.whispertflite.tts;

import android.content.Context;
import android.media.AudioAttributes;
import android.media.AudioFocusRequest;
import android.media.AudioManager;
import android.os.Build;
import android.speech.tts.TextToSpeech;
import android.speech.tts.UtteranceProgressListener;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.UUID;

public class TTSManager {
    public interface Listener {
        void onStart(String utteranceId);
        void onDone(String utteranceId);
        void onError(String utteranceId, String message);
    }

    public enum Mode { FLUSH, QUEUE }
    private final Context appCtx;
    private final AudioManager audio;
    private TextToSpeech tts;
    private Listener listener;

    private float rate = 1.0f;
    private float pitch = 1.0f;
    private boolean enabled = true;
    private boolean mayDuck = true; // transient duck vs full gain
    private Locale locale = Locale.US;
    private AudioFocusRequest focusReq;

    public TTSManager(Context ctx) {
        this.appCtx = ctx.getApplicationContext();
        this.audio = (AudioManager) appCtx.getSystemService(Context.AUDIO_SERVICE);
    }

    public void setListener(Listener l) { this.listener = l; }
    public void setEnabled(boolean e) { this.enabled = e; }
    public void setRate(float r) { this.rate = r; if (tts != null) tts.setSpeechRate(r); }
    public void setPitch(float p) { this.pitch = p; if (tts != null) tts.setPitch(p); }
    public void setMayDuck(boolean duck) { this.mayDuck = duck; }
    public void setLocale(Locale loc) { this.locale = loc; if (tts != null) tts.setLanguage(loc); }

    public void init(Runnable onReady, Runnable onError) {
        if (tts != null) { if (onReady != null) onReady.run(); return; }
        tts = new TextToSpeech(appCtx, status -> {
            if (status == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS) {
                tts.setLanguage(locale);
                tts.setSpeechRate(rate);
                tts.setPitch(pitch);
                tts.setOnUtteranceProgressListener(new UtteranceProgressListener() {
                    @Override public void onStart(String utteranceId) {
                        if (listener != null) listener.onStart(utteranceId);
                    }
                    @Override public void onDone(String utteranceId) {
                        abandonFocus();
                        if (listener != null) listener.onDone(utteranceId);
                    }
                    @Override public void onError(String utteranceId) { onError(utteranceId, "Unknown"); }
                    @Override public void onError(String utteranceId, int errorCode) { onError(utteranceId, String.valueOf(errorCode)); }
                    private void onError(String id, String msg) {
                        abandonFocus();
                        if (listener != null) listener.onError(id, msg);
                    }
                });
                if (onReady != null) onReady.run();
            } else {
                if (onError != null) onError.run();
            }
        });
    }

    public boolean speak(String text, Mode mode) {
        if (!enabled || tts == null) return false;
        requestFocus();
        String id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 21) {
            int queue = (mode == Mode.FLUSH) ? TextToSpeech.QUEUE_FLUSH : TextToSpeech.QUEUE_ADD;
            return tts.speak(text, queue, null, id) == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS;
        } else {
            @SuppressWarnings("deprecation")
            HashMap<String, String> params = new HashMap<>();
            params.put(TextToSpeech.Engine.KEY_PARAM_UTTERANCE_ID, id);
            @SuppressWarnings("deprecation")
            int queue = (mode == Mode.FLUSH) ? TextToSpeech.QUEUE_FLUSH : TextToSpeech.QUEUE_ADD;
            //noinspection deprecation
            return tts.speak(text, queue, params) == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS;
        }
    }

    public void stop() {
        if (tts != null) tts.stop();
        abandonFocus();
    }

    public void shutdown() {
        if (tts != null) {
            tts.shutdown();
            tts = null;
        }
        abandonFocus();
    }

    public Map<String, Locale> listOfflineLocales() {
        Map<String, Locale> out = new HashMap<>();
        if (tts == null) return out;
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 21) {
            for (Locale l : Locale.getAvailableLocales()) {
                int res = tts.isLanguageAvailable(l);
                if (res == TextToSpeech.LANG_AVAILABLE || res == TextToSpeech.LANG_COUNTRY_AVAILABLE || res == TextToSpeech.LANG_COUNTRY_VAR_AVAILABLE) {
                    out.put(l.toLanguageTag(), l);
                }
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    private void requestFocus() {
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26) {
            AudioAttributes attrs = new AudioAttributes.Builder()
                    .setUsage(AudioAttributes.USAGE_ASSISTANCE_ACCESSIBILITY)
                    .setContentType(AudioAttributes.CONTENT_TYPE_SPEECH)
                    .build();
            int gain = mayDuck ? AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK : AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT;
            focusReq = new AudioFocusRequest.Builder(gain)
                    .setOnAudioFocusChangeListener(focusChange -> {})
                    .setAudioAttributes(attrs)
                    .build();
            audio.requestAudioFocus(focusReq);
        } else {
            audio.requestAudioFocus(null, AudioManager.STREAM_MUSIC,
                    mayDuck ? AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK : AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT);
        }
    }

    private void abandonFocus() {
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26 && focusReq != null) audio.abandonAudioFocusRequest(focusReq);
        else audio.abandonAudioFocus(null);
    }
}
````

````java
package com.whispertflite.tts;

import android.content.Context;
import android.media.AudioAttributes;
import android.media.AudioFocusRequest;
import android.media.AudioManager;
import android.os.Build;
import android.speech.tts.TextToSpeech;
import android.speech.tts.UtteranceProgressListener;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.UUID;

public class TTSManager {
    public interface Listener {
        void onStart(String utteranceId);
        void onDone(String utteranceId);
        void onError(String utteranceId, String message);
    }

    public enum Policy { FLUSH, QUEUE }

    private final Context appCtx;
    private final AudioManager audio;
    private TextToSpeech tts;
    private Listener listener;
    private boolean enabled = true;
    private boolean mayDuck = true;
    private AudioFocusRequest focusReq;
    private volatile boolean speaking = false;

    public TTSManager(Context ctx) {
        this.appCtx = ctx.getApplicationContext();
        this.audio = (AudioManager) appCtx.getSystemService(Context.AUDIO_SERVICE);
    }

    public void setListener(Listener l) { this.listener = l; }
    public void setEnabled(boolean e) { this.enabled = e; }
    public boolean isSpeaking() { return speaking; }
    public void setMayDuck(boolean duck) { this.mayDuck = duck; }

    public void init(Runnable onReady, Runnable onError) {
        if (tts != null) { if (onReady != null) onReady.run(); return; }
        tts = new TextToSpeech(appCtx, status -> {
            if (status == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS) {
                tts.setOnUtteranceProgressListener(new UtteranceProgressListener() {
                    @Override public void onStart(String utteranceId) {
                        speaking = true;
                        if (listener != null) listener.onStart(utteranceId);
                    }
                    @Override public void onDone(String utteranceId) {
                        speaking = false;
                        abandonFocus();
                        if (listener != null) listener.onDone(utteranceId);
                    }
                    @Override public void onError(String utteranceId) { handleError(utteranceId, "Unknown"); }
                    @Override public void onError(String utteranceId, int errorCode) { handleError(utteranceId, "code=" + errorCode); }
                    private void handleError(String id, String msg) {
                        speaking = false;
                        abandonFocus();
                        if (listener != null) listener.onError(id, msg);
                    }
                });
                if (onReady != null) onReady.run();
            } else {
                if (onError != null) onError.run();
            }
        });
    }

    public boolean speak(String text, Policy policy) {
        if (!enabled || tts == null || text == null || text.isEmpty()) return false;
        requestFocus();
        String id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        int queueMode = (policy == Policy.FLUSH) ? TextToSpeech.QUEUE_FLUSH : TextToSpeech.QUEUE_ADD;
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 21) {
            return tts.speak(text, queueMode, null, id) == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS;
        } else {
            @SuppressWarnings("deprecation")
            HashMap<String,String> params = new HashMap<>();
            params.put(TextToSpeech.Engine.KEY_PARAM_UTTERANCE_ID, id);
            //noinspection deprecation
            return tts.speak(text, queueMode, params) == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS;
        }
    }

    public void stop() {
        if (tts != null) tts.stop();
        speaking = false;
        abandonFocus();
    }

    public void shutdown() {
        if (tts != null) {
            tts.shutdown();
            tts = null;
        }
        speaking = false;
        abandonFocus();
    }

    private void requestFocus() {
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26) {
            AudioAttributes attrs = new AudioAttributes.Builder()
                    .setUsage(AudioAttributes.USAGE_ASSISTANCE_ACCESSIBILITY)
                    .setContentType(AudioAttributes.CONTENT_TYPE_SPEECH)
                    .build();
            int gain = mayDuck ? AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK : AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT;
            focusReq = new AudioFocusRequest.Builder(gain)
                    .setOnAudioFocusChangeListener(fc -> {})
                    .setAudioAttributes(attrs)
                    .build();
            audio.requestAudioFocus(focusReq);
        } else {
            audio.requestAudioFocus(null, AudioManager.STREAM_MUSIC,
                    mayDuck ? AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK : AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT);
        }
    }

    private void abandonFocus() {
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26 && focusReq != null) audio.abandonAudioFocusRequest(focusReq);
        else audio.abandonAudioFocus(null);
    }
}
````

````java
// ...existing code...
import com.whispertflite.tts.TTSManager;
// ...existing code...
public class MainActivity extends AppCompatActivity {
    // ...existing code...
    private TTSManager tts;
    private boolean prefTtsEnabled = true;
    private String prefTtsInterrupt = "flush"; // "flush" | "queue" | "flush_state"
    private boolean prefTtsDoubleTapStop = true;

    // double-tap detection for earbuds
    private long lastTapMs = 0;
    private static final int DOUBLE_TAP_WINDOW_MS = 350;

    private TTSManager.Policy resolvePolicy(boolean isStateChange) {
        if ("queue".equals(prefTtsInterrupt)) return TTSManager.Policy.QUEUE;
        if ("flush_state".equals(prefTtsInterrupt)) {
            return isStateChange ? TTSManager.Policy.FLUSH : TTSManager.Policy.QUEUE;
        }
        return TTSManager.Policy.FLUSH;
    }

    private void initTTS() {
        tts = new TTSManager(this);
        tts.setEnabled(prefTtsEnabled);
        tts.setListener(new TTSManager.Listener() {
            @Override public void onStart(String id) {
                // Gate mic during TTS
                if (pipelineController != null) pipelineController.onOutputStart();
            }
            @Override public void onDone(String id) {
                if (pipelineController != null) pipelineController.onOutputEnd();
            }
            @Override public void onError(String id, String msg) {
                if (pipelineController != null) pipelineController.onOutputEnd();
            }
        });
        tts.init(null, null);
    }

    private void loadTtsPrefs() {
        SharedPreferences p = PreferenceManager.getDefaultSharedPreferences(this);
        prefTtsEnabled = p.getBoolean("pref_tts_enabled", true);
        prefTtsInterrupt = p.getString("pref_tts_interrupt", "flush");
        prefTtsDoubleTapStop = p.getBoolean("pref_tts_double_tap_stop", true);
        if (tts != null) tts.setEnabled(prefTtsEnabled);
    }

    @Override protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState);
        // ...existing code...
        initTTS();
        loadTtsPrefs();
    }

    @Override protected void onResume() {
        super.onResume();
        // ...existing code...
        loadTtsPrefs();
    }

    // Call this where you announce state changes (not ready/listening earcons)
    private void speakState(String text) {
        if (tts == null || !prefTtsEnabled) return;
        tts.speak(text, resolvePolicy(true));
    }
    private void speakInfo(String text) {
        if (tts == null || !prefTtsEnabled) return;
        tts.speak(text, resolvePolicy(false));
    }

    // Media/earbud handling: double-tap to stop TTS if enabled
    // Hook this into your existing media button callback.
    private boolean onTransportPlayPausePressed() {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (prefTtsDoubleTapStop && tts != null && tts.isSpeaking()) {
            if (now - lastTapMs <= DOUBLE_TAP_WINDOW_MS) {
                tts.stop();
                lastTapMs = 0;
                return true; // consumed
            }
            lastTapMs = now;
        } else {
            lastTapMs = now;
        }
        // ...existing code... toggle listening/session, etc.
        return false;
    }
    // ...existing code...
}
````

Notes and gotchas
- System TTS engine: users can pick sherpaTTS in Android Settings > System > Languages & input > Text-to-speech output. We won’t manage voices/rate/pitch in-app.
- Earcons remain for ready/listening; TTS is for feedback only.
- Audio focus: transient, duck by default; change with setMayDuck(false) if you want strict gain during TTS.
- Double-tap: if a double-tap is also mapped to another action, we consume it only when TTS is speaking and the pref is on.
- App-wide session-listen vs wake-listen: we can move those controls to the AppBar or NavBar next. For now, nothing here changes those; this TTS work is isolated.

````java
package com.whispertflite.ui;

import android.content.Context;
import android.os.Bundle;
import androidx.annotation.NonNull;
import androidx.annotation.Nullable;
import androidx.fragment.app.Fragment;
import android.view.LayoutInflater;
import android.view.View;
import android.view.ViewGroup;
import android.widget.CompoundButton;
import com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton;
import com.google.android.material.switchmaterial.SwitchMaterial;
import com.whispertflite.R;

public class StartFragment extends Fragment {

    public interface Listener {
        void onStartNewChat();
        void onStartNewRecording();
        void onToggleWakeListen(boolean enabled);
        void onToggleSessionListen(boolean enabled);
    }

    private Listener listener;

    @Override public void onAttach(@NonNull Context context) {
        super.onAttach(context);
        if (context instanceof Listener) listener = (Listener) context;
    }
    @Override public void onDetach() {
        super.onDetach();
        listener = null;
    }

    @Nullable @Override
    public View onCreateView(@NonNull LayoutInflater inflater, @Nullable ViewGroup container, @Nullable Bundle savedInstanceState) {
        return inflater.inflate(R.layout.fragment_start, container, false);
    }

    @Override public void onViewCreated(@NonNull View v, @Nullable Bundle savedInstanceState) {
        MaterialButton btnChat = v.findViewById(R.id.btn_new_chat);
        MaterialButton btnRec = v.findViewById(R.id.btn_new_recording);
        SwitchMaterial swWake = v.findViewById(R.id.sw_wake_listen);
        SwitchMaterial swSession = v.findViewById(R.id.sw_session_listen);

        btnChat.setOnClickListener(view -> { if (listener != null) listener.onStartNewChat(); });
        btnRec.setOnClickListener(view -> { if (listener != null) listener.onStartNewRecording(); });

        CompoundButton.OnCheckedChangeListener l = (button, isChecked) -> {
            if (listener == null) return;
            if (button.getId() == R.id.sw_wake_listen) listener.onToggleWakeListen(isChecked);
            else if (button.getId() == R.id.sw_session_listen) listener.onToggleSessionListen(isChecked);
        };
        swWake.setOnCheckedChangeListener(l);
        swSession.setOnCheckedChangeListener(l);
    }
}
````

````java
package com.whispertflite.tts;

import android.content.Context;
import android.media.AudioAttributes;
import android.media.AudioFocusRequest;
import android.media.AudioManager;
import android.os.Build;
import android.speech.tts.TextToSpeech;
import android.speech.tts.UtteranceProgressListener;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.UUID;

public class TTSManager {
    public interface Listener {
        void onStart(String utteranceId);
        void onDone(String utteranceId);
        void onError(String utteranceId, String message);
    }
    public enum Policy { FLUSH, QUEUE }

    private final Context appCtx;
    private final AudioManager audio;
    private TextToSpeech tts;
    private Listener listener;
    private boolean enabled = true;
    private boolean mayDuck = true;
    private AudioFocusRequest focusReq;
    private volatile boolean speaking = false;

    public TTSManager(Context ctx) {
        this.appCtx = ctx.getApplicationContext();
        this.audio = (AudioManager) appCtx.getSystemService(Context.AUDIO_SERVICE);
    }

    public void setListener(Listener l) { this.listener = l; }
    public void setEnabled(boolean e) { this.enabled = e; }
    public boolean isSpeaking() { return speaking; }
    public void setMayDuck(boolean duck) { this.mayDuck = duck; }

    public void init(Runnable onReady, Runnable onError) {
        if (tts != null) { if (onReady != null) onReady.run(); return; }
        tts = new TextToSpeech(appCtx, status -> {
            if (status == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS) {
                try {
                    int avail = tts.isLanguageAvailable(Locale.US);
                    if (avail == TextToSpeech.LANG_AVAILABLE
                            || avail == TextToSpeech.LANG_COUNTRY_AVAILABLE
                            || avail == TextToSpeech.LANG_COUNTRY_VAR_AVAILABLE) {
                        tts.setLanguage(Locale.US);
                    }
                } catch (Throwable ignore) {}
                tts.setOnUtteranceProgressListener(new UtteranceProgressListener() {
                    @Override public void onStart(String utteranceId) {
                        speaking = true;
                        if (listener != null) listener.onStart(utteranceId);
                    }
                    @Override public void onDone(String utteranceId) {
                        speaking = false;
                        abandonFocus();
                        if (listener != null) listener.onDone(utteranceId);
                    }
                    @Override public void onError(String utteranceId) { handleError(utteranceId, "Unknown"); }
                    @Override public void onError(String utteranceId, int errorCode) { handleError(utteranceId, "code=" + errorCode); }
                    private void handleError(String id, String msg) {
                        speaking = false;
                        abandonFocus();
                        if (listener != null) listener.onError(id, msg);
                    }
                });
                if (onReady != null) onReady.run();
            } else {
                if (onError != null) onError.run();
            }
        });
    }

    public boolean speak(String text, Policy policy) {
        if (!enabled || tts == null || text == null || text.isEmpty()) return false;
        requestFocus();
        String id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        int queueMode = (policy == Policy.FLUSH) ? TextToSpeech.QUEUE_FLUSH : TextToSpeech.QUEUE_ADD;
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 21) {
            return tts.speak(text, queueMode, null, id) == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS;
        } else {
            @SuppressWarnings("deprecation")
            HashMap<String,String> params = new HashMap<>();
            params.put(TextToSpeech.Engine.KEY_PARAM_UTTERANCE_ID, id);
            //noinspection deprecation
            return tts.speak(text, queueMode, params) == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS;
        }
    }

    public void stop() {
        if (tts != null) tts.stop();
        speaking = false;
        abandonFocus();
    }

    public void shutdown() {
        if (tts != null) {
            tts.shutdown();
            tts = null;
        }
        speaking = false;
        abandonFocus();
    }

    private void requestFocus() {
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26) {
            AudioAttributes attrs = new AudioAttributes.Builder()
                    .setUsage(AudioAttributes.USAGE_ASSISTANCE_ACCESSIBILITY)
                    .setContentType(AudioAttributes.CONTENT_TYPE_SPEECH)
                    .build();
            int gain = mayDuck ? AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK : AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT;
            focusReq = new AudioFocusRequest.Builder(gain)
                    .setOnAudioFocusChangeListener(fc -> {})
                    .setAudioAttributes(attrs)
                    .build();
            audio.requestAudioFocus(focusReq);
        } else {
            audio.requestAudioFocus(null, AudioManager.STREAM_MUSIC,
                    mayDuck ? AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK : AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT);
        }
    }

    private void abandonFocus() {
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26 && focusReq != null) audio.abandonAudioFocusRequest(focusReq);
        else audio.abandonAudioFocus(null);
    }
}
````

````java
        return TTSManager.Policy.FLUSH;

        tts.speak(text, resolvePolicy(false));
    }
````

````java
    public boolean onTransportPlayPausePressed() {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (prefTtsDoubleTapStop && tts != null && tts.isSpeaking()) {

        return false; // let normal handling proceed
    }

    public boolean handleVoiceCommand(String transcript) {

        String t = transcript.trim().toLowerCase();

            // TODO: navigate to Chat mode / arm chat pipeline

        }
        if (t.contains("start new recording")) {
````

1) New TTS manager

````java
package com.whispertflite.tts;

import android.content.Context;
import android.media.AudioAttributes;
import android.media.AudioFocusRequest;
import android.media.AudioManager;
import android.os.Build;
import android.speech.tts.TextToSpeech;
import android.speech.tts.UtteranceProgressListener;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.UUID;

public class TTSManager {
    public interface Listener {
        void onStart(String utteranceId);
        void onDone(String utteranceId);
        void onError(String utteranceId, String message);
    }
    public enum Policy { FLUSH, QUEUE }

    private final Context appCtx;
    private final AudioManager audio;
    private TextToSpeech tts;
    private Listener listener;
    private boolean enabled = true;
    private boolean mayDuck = true;
    private AudioFocusRequest focusReq;
    private volatile boolean speaking = false;

    public TTSManager(Context ctx) {
        this.appCtx = ctx.getApplicationContext();
        this.audio = (AudioManager) appCtx.getSystemService(Context.AUDIO_SERVICE);
    }

    public void setListener(Listener l) { this.listener = l; }
    public void setEnabled(boolean e) { this.enabled = e; }
    public boolean isSpeaking() { return speaking; }
    public void setMayDuck(boolean duck) { this.mayDuck = duck; }

    public void init(Runnable onReady, Runnable onError) {
        if (tts != null) { if (onReady != null) onReady.run(); return; }
        tts = new TextToSpeech(appCtx, status -> {
            if (status == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS) {
                try {
                    int avail = tts.isLanguageAvailable(Locale.US);
                    if (avail == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS
                            || avail == TextToSpeech.LANG_AVAILABLE
                            || avail == TextToSpeech.LANG_COUNTRY_AVAILABLE
                            || avail == TextToSpeech.LANG_COUNTRY_VAR_AVAILABLE) {
                        tts.setLanguage(Locale.US);
                    }
                } catch (Throwable ignore) {}
                tts.setOnUtteranceProgressListener(new UtteranceProgressListener() {
                    @Override public void onStart(String utteranceId) {
                        speaking = true;
                        if (listener != null) listener.onStart(utteranceId);
                    }
                    @Override public void onDone(String utteranceId) {
                        speaking = false;
                        abandonFocus();
                        if (listener != null) listener.onDone(utteranceId);
                    }
                    @Override public void onError(String utteranceId) { handleError(utteranceId, "Unknown"); }
                    @Override public void onError(String utteranceId, int errorCode) { handleError(utteranceId, "code=" + errorCode); }
                    private void handleError(String id, String msg) {
                        speaking = false;
                        abandonFocus();
                        if (listener != null) listener.onError(id, msg);
                    }
                });
                if (onReady != null) onReady.run();
            } else {
                if (onError != null) onError.run();
            }
        });
    }

    public boolean speak(String text, Policy policy) {
        if (!enabled || tts == null || text == null || text.isEmpty()) return false;
        requestFocus();
        String id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        int queueMode = (policy == Policy.FLUSH) ? TextToSpeech.QUEUE_FLUSH : TextToSpeech.QUEUE_ADD;
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 21) {
            return tts.speak(text, queueMode, null, id) == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS;
        } else {
            @SuppressWarnings("deprecation")
            HashMap<String,String> params = new HashMap<>();
            params.put(TextToSpeech.Engine.KEY_PARAM_UTTERANCE_ID, id);
            //noinspection deprecation
            return tts.speak(text, queueMode, params) == TextToSpeech.SUCCESS;
        }
    }

    public void stop() {
        if (tts != null) tts.stop();
        speaking = false;
        abandonFocus();
    }

    public void shutdown() {
        if (tts != null) {
            tts.shutdown();
            tts = null;
        }
        speaking = false;
        abandonFocus();
    }

    private void requestFocus() {
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26) {
            AudioAttributes attrs = new AudioAttributes.Builder()
                    .setUsage(AudioAttributes.USAGE_ASSISTANCE_ACCESSIBILITY)
                    .setContentType(AudioAttributes.CONTENT_TYPE_SPEECH)
                    .build();
            int gain = mayDuck ? AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK : AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT;
            focusReq = new AudioFocusRequest.Builder(gain)
                    .setOnAudioFocusChangeListener(fc -> {})
                    .setAudioAttributes(attrs)
                    .build();
            audio.requestAudioFocus(focusReq);
        } else {
            audio.requestAudioFocus(null, AudioManager.STREAM_MUSIC,
                    mayDuck ? AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK : AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT);
        }
    }

    private void abandonFocus() {
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26 && focusReq != null) audio.abandonAudioFocusRequest(focusReq);
        else audio.abandonAudioFocus(null);
    }
}
````

````java
// ...existing code...
import android.content.SharedPreferences;
import androidx.preference.PreferenceManager;
import com.whispertflite.tts.TTSManager;
// ...existing code...
public class MainActivity extends AppCompatActivity {
    // ...existing code...
    private TTSManager tts;
    private boolean prefTtsEnabled = true;
    private String prefTtsInterrupt = "flush"; // flush | queue | flush_state
    private boolean prefTtsDoubleTapStop = true;
    private long lastTapMs = 0;
    private static final int DOUBLE_TAP_WINDOW_MS = 350;

    // ...existing code...

    private void initTTS() {
        tts = new TTSManager(this);
        tts.setEnabled(prefTtsEnabled);
        tts.setListener(new TTSManager.Listener() {
            @Override public void onStart(String id) { gateMicStart(); }
            @Override public void onDone(String id) { gateMicEnd(); }
            @Override public void onError(String id, String msg) { gateMicEnd(); }
        });
        tts.init(null, null);
    }

    private void loadTtsPrefs() {
        SharedPreferences p = PreferenceManager.getDefaultSharedPreferences(this);
        prefTtsEnabled = p.getBoolean("pref_tts_enabled", true);
        prefTtsInterrupt = p.getString("pref_tts_interrupt", "flush");
        prefTtsDoubleTapStop = p.getBoolean("pref_tts_double_tap_stop", true);
        if (tts != null) tts.setEnabled(prefTtsEnabled);
    }

    private TTSManager.Policy resolvePolicy(boolean isStateChange) {
        if ("queue".equals(prefTtsInterrupt)) return TTSManager.Policy.QUEUE;
        if ("flush_state".equals(prefTtsInterrupt)) return isStateChange ? TTSManager.Policy.FLUSH : TTSManager.Policy.QUEUE;
        return TTSManager.Policy.FLUSH;
    }

    private void speakState(String text) {
        if (tts == null || !prefTtsEnabled) return;
        tts.speak(text, resolvePolicy(true));
    }
    private void speakInfo(String text) {
        if (tts == null || !prefTtsEnabled) return;
        tts.speak(text, resolvePolicy(false));
    }

    // Call from media transport play/pause to support double-tap stop
    public boolean onTransportPlayPausePressed() {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (prefTtsDoubleTapStop && tts != null && tts.isSpeaking()) {
            if (now - lastTapMs <= DOUBLE_TAP_WINDOW_MS) {
                tts.stop();
                lastTapMs = 0;
                return true; // consumed
            }
            lastTapMs = now;
        } else {
            lastTapMs = now;
        }
        return false;
    }

    // Voice command router (call from ASR finalize)
    public boolean handleVoiceCommand(String transcript) {
        if (transcript == null) return false;
        String t = transcript.trim().toLowerCase();
        if (t.contains("start new chat")) {
            // TODO: navigate/arm chat mode
            speakState("Chat mode.");
            return true;
        }
        if (t.contains("start new recording")) {
            // TODO: navigate/start recording mode
            speakState("Starting a new recording.");
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    // Mic gating via reflection to avoid hard compile dependency on method names
    private void gateMicStart() {
        try {
            Object pc = /* ...existing code... */ pipelineController;
            if (pc != null) pc.getClass().getMethod("onOutputStart").invoke(pc);
        } catch (Throwable ignored) {}
    }
    private void gateMicEnd() {
        try {
            Object pc = /* ...existing code... */ pipelineController;
            if (pc != null) pc.getClass().getMethod("onOutputEnd").invoke(pc);
        } catch (Throwable ignored) {}
    }

    @Override protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState);
        // ...existing code...
        loadTtsPrefs();
        initTTS();
    }
````

_**Assistant**_

Yes.

- WebRTC/Android VAD
  - Classic C VAD used across Android/WebRTC; 10/20/30 ms frames at 8/16/32 kHz; “aggressiveness” 0–3.
  - Very low CPU, tiny latency, BSD-like license. Good for gating wakeword/session quickly.
  - JNI wrapper or existing Android ports are common. Fits our 16 kHz / 20 ms frames directly.

- Silero VAD
  - Neural VAD (PyTorch), robust in noise; outputs speech probability per frame/window (~30 ms).
  - Runs on-device via ONNX Runtime Mobile (or NCNN/TFLite after conversion). Model ~1–3 MB.
  - Slightly higher CPU/latency than WebRTC VAD but usually better accuracy in real environments.

- Trade-offs
  - WebRTC VAD: fastest, smallest; less robust in very noisy/echoey rooms.
  - Silero VAD: more robust, modest CPU hit; tune threshold + hangover for no-barge-in.

If you want, I can swap our `VadEnergy` for WebRTC VAD first (minimal change), or add Silero VAD behind a Settings toggle and wire it into the same PipelineController.

Got it. Here’s a quick, practical breakdown of what you’re running now vs. a true WebRTC VAD via JNI, and why you’re seeing the accuracy jump.

## What you have now (Java heuristic “WebRTC-like”)
- Features used: RMS energy + Zero-Crossing Rate with simple hysteresis (attack/hangover).
- Decision granularity: per 20 ms frame (matches your pipeline).
- Strengths:
  - Kills a lot of low-energy/steady noise the energy VAD let through.
  - ZCR helps reject hum/AC/fan and accept voiced segments → fewer false triggers.
- Limitations:
  - No multi-band analysis; no trained models; no noise adaptation.
  - Performance varies with environment; more fragile in non-stationary noise.
  - No “aggressiveness” modes; threshold is a single scalar.

## True WebRTC VAD (JNI)
- Algorithm: Production-grade VAD from WebRTC’s common_audio/vad.
  - Multi-band energy features + decision logic designed for telephony/RTC.
  - Tunable aggressiveness modes (0–3) to trade recall vs. precision.
  - Per-frame decisions (10/20/30 ms) at 8/16/32/48 kHz; best at 10–20 ms.
- API surface:
  - Init, SetMode(0–3), Process(sampleRate, frameInt16) → 1 (speech) / 0 (non-speech).
  - Low-latency, deterministic, very fast (tiny CPU).
- Strengths:
  - Robust to varied noise, different speakers, far-field mics.
  - Stable segment boundaries; fewer split utterances.
  - Widely deployed and battle-tested.
- Considerations:
  - Needs JNI shim and bundling the small C module.
  - Works on int16 PCM; you’ll convert your float frames once per frame (cheap).
  - Your external attack/hangover is still useful; “Threshold” slider becomes mostly irrelevant, replaced by WebRTC “aggressiveness.”

## Why you saw big gains
- Energy-only VAD let through “loud but non-speech” frames; Whisper got junk onset/offsets → worse transcripts.
- Adding ZCR filtered many of those non-speech frames, making captured segments cleaner → Whisper sees better SNR content → higher accuracy.
- WebRTC VAD goes farther: it uses multi-band stats and tuned decision rules, so you get this effect consistently across more conditions.

## Mapping to your Settings
- Engine = Energy | WebRTC | Silero (in place).
- With WebRTC:
  - Keep Attack/Hangover, Pre-roll, In-capture silence, Cooldown, Max capture.
  - Replace “Threshold” with “Aggressiveness” (0–3). Threshold can be hidden or left inert for this engine.
- No-barge-in, arming delay, cooldown, and earcons remain unchanged.

## Integration plan (minimal)
- Add WebRTC VAD sources (common_audio/vad/*) to your `` and CMake.
- JNI wrapper: init, setMode(int), process(short[], sr, frameLen).
- Java class `VadWebRtcNative implements BasicVad`:
  - Convert float[] → short[] (fast loop) and call native `process`.
  - Mirror your current listener callbacks.
- Use your existing segmented toggle to select it; add a “VAD aggressiveness” ListPreference when WebRTC is selected.

## Trade-offs at a glance
- Java heuristic: zero deps, good quick win, inconsistent in tough noise.
- WebRTC (JNI): tiny native dep, much more robust, tunable, near-zero CPU overhead.
